title: Change of Base

blocks.html: Calculators have keys for $\log$ (base 10) and $\ln$ (base $e$), but not for $\log_7$. The power rule lets you rewrite any log in a base you have.
$$\log_b x = \frac{\log_c x}{\log_c b}$$ for any allowed base $c$. Usually $c = 10$ or $c = e$: $\log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$.

Let $y = \log_b x$, so $b^y = x$. Take $\ln$ of both sides: $\ln(b^y) = \ln x$. The power rule gives $y\ln b = \ln x$, so $y = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$. This also shows that every log function is a constant multiple of $\ln x$: their graphs are vertical stretches of one another.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b} = \log_b x$ and $g(x) = \ln x$. Changing the base only stretches the graph vertically; every log crosses the $x$-axis at 1.

blocks.html: Which base should you change to? Any base works, so pick a convenient one: base 10 or $e$ for a calculator, or a shared base (like 2 for $\log_8 32$) to get an exact answer by hand.

blocks.title: A base without a calculator key
blocks.q: Find $\log_2 10$ to two decimal places, and use it to estimate $\log_2 1000$.

blocks.html: Flipping the fraction: $\log_3 20 = \frac{\ln 3}{\ln 20}$ is wrong (it gives about $0.37$). The number you are taking the log of goes on top. A sanity check: $3^2 = 9$ and $3^3 = 27$, so $\log_3 20$ must be between 2 and 3.
